--- title: "S0-01 notebook — R" subtitle: "Compartments and ODEs from first principles" execute: freeze: auto --- Everything in the lesson, built from scratch and checked. Run it top to bottom. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(deSolve) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11)) ``` ::: ## 1. One compartment, IV bolus — and a check you should always run Work in **amounts** inside the ODE and convert to concentration at the end. Doses in µg with volumes in L means µg/L, which reads directly as ng/mL. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} CL <- 12; V <- 60 # L/h, L D <- 50 * 1000 # 50 mg as ug k <- CL / V t <- seq(0, 48, by = 0.1) sol <- ode(c(A = D), t, function(t, y, p) list(-k * y["A"]), parms = NULL, method = "lsoda", rtol = 1e-10, atol = 1e-12) numeric <- sol[, "A"] / V analytic <- (D / V) * exp(-k * t) cat(sprintf("max relative error vs analytic : %.2e\n", max(abs(numeric - analytic) / analytic))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` max relative error vs analytic : 9.75e-11 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("half-life : %.2f h\n", log(2) / k)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` half-life : 3.47 h ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("AUC(0-inf) numeric : %.1f ng*h/mL\n", sum(diff(t) * (head(numeric, -1) + tail(numeric, -1)) / 2) + tail(numeric, 1) / k)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AUC(0-inf) numeric : 4166.8 ng*h/mL ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("D / CL : %.1f ng*h/mL\n", D / CL)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` D / CL : 4166.7 ng*h/mL ``` ::: ::: Two habits worth forming now. **Always validate numerics against an analytical solution when one exists.** And **`AUC(0-inf) = D/CL` is exact for any linear model**, so it is a free correctness check on every simulation you ever write. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(t = t, conc = numeric) |> ggplot(aes(t, conc)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + scale_y_log10() + labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Conc (ng/mL)", title = "Semi-log — a straight line") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](notebook-r_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 2. Add absorption ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} one_cmt_oral <- function(t, y, p) with(as.list(c(y, p)), { list(c(A_gut = -ka * A_gut, A_c = ka * A_gut - (CL / V) * A_c)) }) ka <- 1.2 tt <- seq(0, 48, by = 0.01) s <- ode(c(A_gut = D, A_c = 0), tt, one_cmt_oral, parms = c(ka = ka, CL = CL, V = V), method = "lsoda", rtol = 1e-10, atol = 1e-12) cc <- s[, "A_c"] / V cat(sprintf("tmax numeric %.3f h analytic %.3f h Cmax %.1f ng/mL\n", tt[which.max(cc)], log(ka / k) / (ka - k), max(cc))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` tmax numeric 1.790 h analytic 1.792 h Cmax 582.4 ng/mL ``` ::: ::: ### Flip-flop: when the terminal slope is absorption ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (ka_i in c(1.2, 0.05)) { tg <- seq(0, 120, by = 0.1) si <- ode(c(A_gut = D, A_c = 0), tg, one_cmt_oral, parms = c(ka = ka_i, CL = CL, V = V), method = "lsoda", rtol = 1e-10, atol = 1e-12) ci <- si[, "A_c"] / V m <- tg > 72 & ci > 0 slope <- coef(lm(log(ci[m]) ~ tg[m]))[2] cat(sprintf("ka = %5.2f /h -> terminal t1/2 from slope = %5.2f h\n", ka_i, log(2) / -slope)) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ka = 1.20 /h -> terminal t1/2 from slope = 3.47 h ka = 0.05 /h -> terminal t1/2 from slope = 13.86 h ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("\nelimination t1/2 = %.2f h absorption t1/2 (ka = 0.05) = %.2f h\n", log(2) / k, log(2) / 0.05)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` elimination t1/2 = 3.47 h absorption t1/2 (ka = 0.05) = 13.86 h ``` ::: ::: The slow-absorption curve's terminal slope reports the **absorption** half-life, not the elimination half-life. Nothing in the fit tells you which one you are looking at. Only an IV arm does. ## 3. Two compartments — the CASE-SM structure ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hybrid <- function(CL, Vc, Q, Vp) { k10 <- CL / Vc; k12 <- Q / Vc; k21 <- Q / Vp s <- k10 + k12 + k21 d <- sqrt(s^2 - 4 * k10 * k21) c(alpha = (s + d) / 2, beta = (s - d) / 2, k21 = k21) } conc_sd <- function(t, dose_mg, ka, CL, Vc, Q, Vp) { h <- hybrid(CL, Vc, Q, Vp); a <- h["alpha"]; b <- h["beta"]; k21 <- h["k21"] A <- dose_mg * 1000 * ka / Vc as.numeric(A * (((k21 - a) / ((ka - a) * (b - a))) * exp(-a * t) + ((k21 - b) / ((ka - b) * (a - b))) * exp(-b * t) + ((k21 - ka) / ((a - ka) * (b - ka))) * exp(-ka * t))) } TRUE_P <- list(ka = 1.2, CL = 12, Vc = 60, Q = 8, Vp = 90) # CASE-SM typical values ode_sd <- function(t, dose_mg, ka, CL, Vc, Q, Vp) { rhs <- function(t, y, p) with(as.list(y), list(c( A_gut = -ka * A_gut, A_c = ka * A_gut - (CL / Vc) * A_c - (Q / Vc) * A_c + (Q / Vp) * A_p, A_p = (Q / Vc) * A_c - (Q / Vp) * A_p))) s <- ode(c(A_gut = dose_mg * 1000, A_c = 0, A_p = 0), c(0, t), rhs, parms = NULL, method = "lsoda", rtol = 1e-11, atol = 1e-13) (s[-1, "A_c"]) / Vc } tg <- seq(0.01, 72, length.out = 200) an <- do.call(conc_sd, c(list(t = tg, dose_mg = 50), TRUE_P)) nu <- do.call(ode_sd, c(list(t = tg, dose_mg = 50), TRUE_P)) h <- hybrid(TRUE_P$CL, TRUE_P$Vc, TRUE_P$Q, TRUE_P$Vp) cat(sprintf("analytic vs ODE, max relative error : %.1e\n", max(abs(an - nu) / nu))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` analytic vs ODE, max relative error : 1.2e-10 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("distribution t1/2 (alpha) : %.2f h\n", log(2) / h["alpha"])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` distribution t1/2 (alpha) : 1.85 h ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("terminal t1/2 (beta) : %.2f h\n", log(2) / h["beta"])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` terminal t1/2 (beta) : 14.61 h ``` ::: ::: Two half-lives, differing eight-fold. Quoting "the" half-life of this compound without saying which one is meaningless. ## 4. Multiple dosing by superposition For a **linear** model the response to repeated doses is the sum of the responses to each dose alone — not an approximation. It gives you a fast simulator and an exact check at once. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} conc_md <- function(t, dose_mg, ka, CL, Vc, Q, Vp, n_doses = 21, tau = 24) { out <- numeric(length(t)) for (i in seq_len(n_doses) - 1) { dt <- t - i * tau ok <- dt >= 0 if (any(ok)) out[ok] <- out[ok] + conc_sd(dt[ok], dose_mg, ka, CL, Vc, Q, Vp) } out } trapz <- function(x, y) sum(diff(x) * (head(y, -1) + tail(y, -1)) / 2) g1 <- seq(0, 24, length.out = 24001) gss <- seq(480, 504, length.out = 24001) auc1 <- trapz(g1, do.call(conc_md, c(list(t = g1, dose_mg = 50), TRUE_P))) css <- do.call(conc_md, c(list(t = gss, dose_mg = 50), TRUE_P)) aucss <- trapz(gss, css) cat(sprintf("AUC(0-24) day 1 : %8.1f ng*h/mL\n", auc1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AUC(0-24) day 1 : 3424.3 ng*h/mL ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("AUC(tau) steady state : %8.1f ng*h/mL\n", aucss)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AUC(tau) steady state : 4166.7 ng*h/mL ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("Dose / CL : %8.1f ng*h/mL <- must match exactly\n", 50000 / TRUE_P$CL)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Dose / CL : 4166.7 ng*h/mL <- must match exactly ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("accumulation ratio : %8.3f\n", aucss / auc1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` accumulation ratio : 1.217 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("steady-state Cmax %.1f, Cmin %.1f ng/mL\n", max(css), min(css))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` steady-state Cmax 560.7, Cmin 51.9 ng/mL ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tf <- seq(0, 504, by = 0.1) tibble(day = tf / 24, conc = do.call(conc_md, c(list(t = tf, dose_mg = 50), TRUE_P))) |> filter(conc > 0) |> ggplot(aes(day, conc)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) + scale_y_log10() + labs(x = "Day", y = "Conc (ng/mL)", title = "CASE-SM, 50 mg once daily — approach to steady state") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](notebook-r_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Note how quickly the troughs plateau despite a 14.6 h terminal half-life: the accumulation ratio is 1.22, not the ~3 that a single-exponential intuition would predict. ## 5. Failure mode — a converged, meaningless fit ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df <- read.csv("../../cases/case-sm/data/ozanib_pk.csv") truth <- read.csv("../../cases/case-sm/data/ozanib_individual_truth.csv") obs <- df |> filter(EVID == 0, !is.na(DV), DAY == 1, TIME > 0) sid <- obs |> count(ID) |> slice_max(n, n = 1) |> pull(ID) |> first() sub <- obs |> filter(ID == sid) dose <- sub$DOSE[1] tr <- truth |> filter(ID == sid) sparse <- sub |> filter(TIME %in% c(0.5, 4, 12)) obj <- function(logp, tt, yy) { p <- exp(pmin(pmax(logp, -6), 8)) pred <- pmax(conc_sd(tt, dose, p[1], p[2], p[3], p[4], p[5]), 1e-8) sum((log(pred) - log(yy))^2) } p0 <- log(c(1, 10, 50, 6, 80)) cat(sprintf("subject %d at %g mg\n", sid, dose)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` subject 1 at 25 mg ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("%-18s ka %5.2f CL %6.2f Vc %6.1f Q %6.2f Vp %7.1f\n", "TRUTH", tr$KA, tr$CL, tr$VC, tr$Q, tr$VP)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` TRUTH ka 1.27 CL 19.25 Vc 88.6 Q 11.84 Vp 151.7 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} for (nm in c("rich", "sparse")) { d <- if (nm == "rich") sub else sparse fit <- optim(p0, obj, tt = d$TIME, yy = d$DV, method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 5000, reltol = 1e-12)) e <- exp(fit$par) cat(sprintf("%-18s ka %5.2f CL %6.2f Vc %6.1f Q %6.2f Vp %7.1f | rmse(log) %.3f\n", sprintf("%s, %d points", nm, nrow(d)), e[1], e[2], e[3], e[4], e[5], sqrt(fit$value / nrow(d)))) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rich, 8 points ka 1.03 CL 28.69 Vc 72.8 Q 24.64 Vp 51.0 | rmse(log) 0.117 sparse, 3 points ka 1.35 CL 31.59 Vc 107.7 Q 18.24 Vp 88.3 | rmse(log) 0.000 ``` ::: ::: The three-point fit reaches a residual error of essentially **zero**: five parameters passing through three points can always be made to fit perfectly, and the optimiser reports success. The rich fit is honest but still recovers `Q` and `Vp` poorly from eight oral samples in one individual — which is not a bug in your code, but the reason population modeling (`S2`) exists. ::: {.callout-important} Convergence is not evidence. A perfect fit is a warning sign rather than a triumph. Look at parameter correlations and conditioning before you look at the estimates. ::: ## 6. A trap that is really in the data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predose <- df |> filter(EVID == 0, DAY == 1, TIME == 0) cat(sprintf("pre-dose samples: %d flagged BLQ: %d reported as a real number: %d\n", nrow(predose), sum(predose$BLQ), sum(!is.na(predose$DV)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` pre-dose samples: 60 flagged BLQ: 58 reported as a real number: 2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} predose |> filter(!is.na(DV)) |> select(ID, TIME, DV, IPRED_TRUE, BLQ) |> head(8) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| ID| TIME| DV| IPRED_TRUE| BLQ| |--:|----:|------:|----------:|---:| | 29| 0| 1.4749| 0| 0| | 43| 0| 1.1808| 0| 0|
::: ::: The true concentration before the first dose is exactly zero, but the assay has additive error, so some pre-dose samples come back as small positive numbers. Feed one into a log-scale objective and it contributes a residual of about 18 and drags the whole fit with it. That is why section 5 filters `TIME > 0`. `S0-03` is about catching this class of problem before it reaches the model. ## What to try next 1. Refit the rich profile with `Q` and `Vp` fixed at the truth. How much better are `CL` and `Vc`? That is the value of borrowing strength, measured. 2. Simulate a missed dose on day 10 (drop one term from the superposition sum) and see how long the trough takes to recover. 3. Set `ka = 0.15` and refit. Can you tell from the fit alone that you are in flip-flop?
